section: The seven papers nobody has pulled (item 2)
sentence_as_it_stands: Wightman & Vaughan 1976. Comparison of compounds used for intradermal anesthesia. Anesthesiology 45(6):687–9. PMID 791022. Unread; no abstract exists. Indexed with benzyl alcohols, parabens, procaine, lidocaine, sodium chloride and injections, intradermal. What it would settle: whether the methylparaben in your vial does anything comparable to the benzyl alcohol in the 1994 trial. This is the highest-value paper in the queue, because the preservative question above turns on it and on nothing else.
quote: Methylparaben did not alter the duration or intensity of anesthesia.
corrected_wording: Wightman & Vaughan 1976. Comparison of compounds used for intradermal anesthesia. Anesthesiology 45(6):687–9. PMID 791022. Read in full from page images, October 2026; no abstract exists. A randomised, double-blind within-subject comparison of six intradermal solutions in 20 volunteers, each his own control, with discomfort on injection rated on a stated scale and anaesthesia timed by pin prick from fifteen seconds to a twenty-minute window. On the preservative question it reports that methylparaben did not alter the duration or intensity of anaesthesia, and did not alter the incidence of discomfort. It does not answer the comparison with the 1994 trial directly, because its benzyl alcohol arm was benzyl alcohol in saline rather than benzyl alcohol added to lidocaine.
notes: The page names this paper the highest-value item in its retrieval queue and says the preservative question turns on it and on nothing else, so the status line and the 'what it would settle' line both need replacing. The answer it gives is a null result for methylparaben on duration, intensity and discomfort, which lowers rather than raises the weight of the record's open product-label question about which preservative is in a given vial. This is the same sentence family as claim C038, which the lead session re-judged from confirmed to refuted.

section: What is still unknown — Whether methylparaben does anything for duration
sentence_as_it_stands: Whether methylparaben does anything for duration. Your vial contains it at [dose figure omitted]. No study compares a methylparaben-preserved lidocaine against a preservative-free or benzyl-alcohol-preserved one for intradermal duration. What would settle it: Wightman and Vaughan 1976, which tested benzyl alcohol, parabens, procaine, lidocaine and saline intradermally in the same design.
quote: Methylparaben did not alter the duration or intensity of anesthesia.
corrected_wording: Whether methylparaben does anything for duration: answered for the preservative-free comparison and still open for the benzyl-alcohol one. Wightman and Vaughan 1976 (PMID 791022) compared a methylparaben-preserved lidocaine against the same lidocaine without preservative as intradermal wheals in 20 volunteers, timed by pin prick within a twenty-minute window, and reported that methylparaben did not alter the duration or intensity of anaesthesia. No study compares a methylparaben-preserved lidocaine against a benzyl-alcohol-preserved one, because the 1976 paper's benzyl alcohol arm was in saline rather than in lidocaine.
notes: The concentration in the second sentence is replaced with [dose figure omitted] under the writing rules. This is the open question the paper was pulled to answer, and the answer splits the claim: the preservative-free limb is settled and the benzyl-alcohol limb is untouched.

section: Is it already in what you are buying? — What follows for you, in order (item 2)
sentence_as_it_stands: Do not assume methylparaben does the same thing. It is a different molecule with different anesthetic properties, and no study in this literature has compared a methylparaben-preserved lidocaine against a benzyl-alcohol-preserved one for duration. The one paper that tested benzyl alcohol, parabens, procaine, lidocaine and saline side by side intradermally is Wightman and Vaughan 1976, and it has never been opened — which makes it the single most decision-relevant unread paper in this seam.
quote: Methylparaben preservative in lidocaine multidose vials did not alter the incidence of discomfort.
corrected_wording: No study in this literature has compared a methylparaben-preserved lidocaine against a benzyl-alcohol-preserved one for duration. The one paper that tested benzyl alcohol, parabens, procaine, lidocaine and saline side by side intradermally is Wightman and Vaughan 1976 (PMID 791022), now read: it reported that methylparaben altered neither the duration nor the intensity of anaesthesia, nor the incidence of discomfort on injection, and that its benzyl alcohol arm was benzyl alcohol in saline rather than in lidocaine.
notes: The clause 'it has never been opened' is out of date and the sentence it sits in is the record's own reason for treating the preservative question as unresolved. The surrounding passage carries an own-use marker dated 2026-10-01 saying it is the user's own use and not research; the correction is to the literature statement inside it, not to the own-use material. Same sentence family as claim C038.

sentence_as_it_stands: Any measurement of injected local anesthetic damage to nerve fibers in skin. The irritancy findings here are bleeding and bruising scored by eye.
quote: Reactions, consisting of localized itching, erythema, and pseudopod formation, appeared in eight of 20 subjects given procaine, but in no other subject.

The visible local-effect findings here are not all bleeding and bruising: Wightman and Vaughan 1976 observed injection sites for adverse local effects and recorded a wheal-and-flare pattern of localised itching, erythema and pseudopod formation after one of its six solutions and after none of the others.
notes: The nerve-fibre absence in this bullet is intact; this paper counted no fibres and took no biopsy. What is understated is the kind of visible local effect this literature has recorded. Recorded against claim C046, and connected to the procaine-page finding below.

sentence_as_it_stands: Against that reputation stands the only controlled dataset on intracutaneous ester exposure, and it is directly about this route.
quote: Reactions, consisting of localized itching, erythema, and pseudopod formation, appeared in eight of 20 subjects given procaine, but in no other subject.
corrected_wording: Against that reputation stand two controlled datasets on intracutaneous ester exposure, and they point in different directions. Weinschenk 2017 observed no type-1 allergy across intracutaneous procaine, lidocaine, mepivacaine and saline, reading the larger procaine wheals as vasodilatation. Wightman and Vaughan 1976 (PMID 791022), randomised, double-blind and within-subject in 20 volunteers, recorded localised itching, erythema and pseudopod formation after procaine in eight of 20 subjects and after none of the other five solutions, and its authors attribute reactions of that kind to the ester-linked group.
notes: The page reads a single reassuring dataset as showing that the ester group's measured record is better than its reputation, and that reading feeds the 'gentlest' entries in its own ranking table and in the comparing page's. A second controlled dataset on the same route exists and reports a local-reaction rate for the ester and for nothing else tested. Weinschenk watched for fifteen minutes only, which the page's own Limits line records, so the two are not measuring quite the same window. Recorded against claim D055; no threshold, ceiling or toxicity figure is reproduced here.

section: What “without a vasoconstrictor” has to mean; The adjuvant already in the bottle
sentence_as_it_stands: Benzyl alcohol is a weak local anesthetic in its own right, not a modifier of another drug. No vessel. / Benzyl alcohol on its own wears off faster than lidocaine. It is an additive, not a substitute.
quote: Satisfactory anesthesia began to dissipate after 2 to 3 minutes with benzyl alcohol–saline solution, after 5 minutes with procaine, and after 20 minutes with the lidocaine preparations
corrected_wording: No change needed. Both statements now have a second, independent human intradermal source: in Wightman and Vaughan 1976 (PMID 791022) benzyl alcohol in saline produced anaesthesia of its own where plain saline produced none, and that anaesthesia began to dissipate within a few minutes against twenty minutes for the lidocaine preparations in the same subjects.
notes: Recorded as now-verified because the page states both points from a single trial each and neither was marked as replicated. The 1976 measurement is of benzyl alcohol in saline rather than added to lidocaine, so it verifies the 'anaesthetic in its own right' and 'wears off faster' statements and not the prolongation figure. Recorded against claims C013 and D019. Two separate sentences from the same page, from the two sections named, joined with a slash; each was checked verbatim against the fetched page.

section: Moffitt 2001, intradermal ropivacaine — Saline was not inert
sentence_as_it_stands: Saline was not inert. “Normal saline produced a degree of partial anesthesia,” and full anaesthesia was reached in one control infiltration after 100 seconds and lasted 20 minutes. INFERENCE A [dose figure omitted] intradermal bleb of saline can abolish pinprick by itself — presumably mechanically — which is a caution about every pinprick-based duration figure from large-volume wheals.
quote: The latter produced poor to no anesthesia (scores 1 to 0) in 85 per cent of subjects.
corrected_wording: No change needed; the volume qualifier is correct and now measured rather than inferred. At a wheal volume, saline alone gave poor to no anaesthesia in most subjects and was the most uncomfortable of six intradermal solutions to inject (Wightman and Vaughan 1976, PMID 791022), which confines the caution to the large-volume blebs the page attaches it to.
notes: The page marks the generalisation as an inference from a single control infiltration. Wightman and Vaughan tested saline as a wheal in 20 volunteers against five other solutions and found it anaesthetically inert, which supports the page's own restriction of the caution to large volumes. Read from the local copy at notion_pages/ropivacaine.md rather than re-fetched; page_version is the 'as of' time inside that file. Volume replaced with [dose figure omitted]. The provenance of the opposing claim is recorded as an extra study: the 1976 paper was written to test a 1976 letter asserting saline is a satisfactory discomfort-free local anaesthetic (PMID 1246252), and it rejected it.
